1.e4 e5.strategy: Claims the centre with a pawn and opens lines for the queen and the king's bishop, mirroring White's move. Black aims for quick development and early castling, while the e5-pawn is a target that White can attack at once. Play is often open, and White keeps the first-move initiative.

1.e4 c5.strategy: Fights for d4 from the flank instead of mirroring White. If White opens the centre, Black trades a wing pawn for a central one, which gives a central majority and a half-open c-file. White usually leads in development and attacks the kingside, Black counterattacks on the queenside, and the unbalanced structure gives both sides winning chances.

1.e4 e6.strategy: Prepares ...d5 with the e-pawn behind it and accepts a slightly cramped position in return for a resilient structure. The c8-bishop is hemmed in by the e6-pawn and often has to be traded or rerouted, but Black has clear plans against White's centre with ...c5. The result is a sound game, at the price of some passivity.

1.e4 c6.strategy: Prepares ...d5 while keeping the c8-bishop free to come out before ...e6, so Black gets a sound pawn structure without a passive light-squared bishop. The price is time: the knight loses its natural c6-square. White usually gets more space and freer development, while Black relies on a solid structure with few weaknesses.

1.e4 d5.strategy: Challenges e4 at once and trades Black's d-pawn for White's e-pawn. Black gets an open game and easy development, but recapturing costs time, so Black gives up some tempi and space for it.

1.e4 d6.strategy: Prepares to develop the knight and fianchetto the king's bishop, and invites White to build a broad centre, which Black then undermines with pawn breaks. The set-up is flexible and keeps many pawn structures possible, but White gets space and attacking chances if Black reacts passively.

1.e4 Nf6.strategy: Attacks e4 at once and invites White to advance the pawn, hoping the advanced pawns become targets. White gains space and tempi by chasing the knight, and Black gets counterplay against the overextended centre. The game is double-edged.

1.e4 g6.strategy: Prepares ...Bg7 to hit White's centre from a distance and keeps the choice of set-up open until White commits. Black accepts less space for a flexible set-up with counterplay later. The risk is a passive position if White builds a big centre and Black does not strike back in time.

1.e4 Nc6.strategy: Develops a knight at once and invites White to build a pawn centre that Black then challenges. The knight blocks the c-pawn, so the usual ...c6 and ...c5 breaks are unavailable, and White keeps more space. Sound, but it gives White the easier game.

1.e4 b6.strategy: Prepares ...Bb7 to press on e4 and the long diagonal, but leaves the centre to White, who can build a broad pawn centre against it. Theory regards the move as unreliable rather than refuted, since the bishop's pressure seldom makes up for the space conceded.

1.e4 a6.name: St. George Defence
1.e4 a6.background: The first known game with 1.e4 a6 was a simultaneous exhibition on 11 December 1868, in which the English amateur J. Baker beat Wilhelm Steinitz. Tony Miles beat Anatoly Karpov with it at the 1980 European Team Championship in Skara, after which it was also called the Birmingham Defence, after Miles's hometown.
1.e4 a6.strategy: Prepares ...b5 and ...Bb7 to attack the centre from the flank, and keeps the choice of set-up open. White simply takes space, and the slow a-pawn move needs ...b5 to justify its tempo. Sound enough, but Black has spent a tempo and conceded the centre.

1.e4 h6.name: Carr Defence
1.e4 h6.background: The defence is mentioned in Unorthodox Chess Openings, and Michael Basman and Magnus Carlsen have both played it.
1.e4 h6.strategy: Spends a tempo on a rook's pawn to prevent Bg5 and prepare ...g5, but does nothing for the centre or development. White has a free hand in the centre, and a follow-up ...g5 only adds a weakened kingside.

1.e4 Na6.name: Lemming Defence
1.e4 Na6.strategy: Sends the knight to the edge, where it does nothing for the centre and can be exchanged by Bxa6 bxa6, which doubles the a-pawns. White takes the centre at leisure while the knight still looks for a useful square.

1.e4 Nh6.name: Adams Defence
1.e4 Nh6.strategy: Puts the knight on the rim, where it covers f5 and g4 but becomes a target: after d4 the bishop on c1 can take it with Bxh6 gxh6 and wreck Black's kingside pawns. Black also spends time without helping the centre.

1.e4 a5.name: Ware Defence
1.e4 a5.background: Also known as the Corn Stalk Defence. Preston Ware, an American player who often played uncommon openings, used it in eleven recorded tournament games from 1880 to 1882, winning four and losing seven.
1.e4 a5.strategy: A rook's pawn move that neither challenges the centre nor develops a piece, and it weakens b5. White takes the centre at leisure and Black has no compensation for the lost time.

1.e4 b5.name: O'Neill Gambit
1.e4 b5.strategy: Offers the b-pawn: 2.Bxb5 wins it at once, and the compensation, ...Bb7 against e4 and the half-open b-file, is too little, since White defends e4 easily and stays a clean pawn up.

1.e4 f6.name: Barnes Defence
1.e4 f6.background: Named after Thomas Wilson Barnes, who beat Paul Morphy with it in 1858, although it is regarded as clearly inferior.
1.e4 f6.strategy: Blocks the natural f6 square of the king's knight and weakens the e8–h5 diagonal and the king. White takes the centre and develops freely, while Black has no useful follow-up.

1.e4 f5.name: Duras Gambit
1.e4 f5.background: The line was played three times in an exhibition match between Ossip Bernstein and Oldřich Duras, after whom the gambit is named.
1.e4 f5.strategy: Offers a pawn: after 2.exf5 Black gets a modest lead in development with ...Nf6 but little else for it, and the e8–h5 diagonal and the king stay weakened.

1.e4 g5.name: Borg Defence
1.e4 g5.background: The name is “Grob” spelled backwards. Michael Basman often played it, and it is also called the Basman Defence; Modern Chess Openings judges Black only somewhat worse, although the move weakens the kingside severely.
1.e4 g5.strategy: Gains kingside space at the price of a lasting weakness: after 2.d4 the bishop on c1 attacks the g5-pawn at once, and the squares around Black's king stay weak for the rest of the game.

1.e4 h5.name: Goldsmith Defence
1.e4 h5.background: Also called the Pickering Defence, it is the Kádas Opening (1.h4) with the colours reversed. Modern Chess Openings dismisses it: “Other defenses, such as 1...h5, are not considered as they are simply too bad and need no discussion.”
1.e4 h5.strategy: Wastes a tempo and weakens g5 and the whole kingside for no gain: the pawn does nothing for the centre or development, and White simply takes the centre.

1.e4.name: King's Pawn Game
1.e4.background: The most popular first move in chess. Bobby Fischer called it “best by test” in My 60 Memorable Games (1969).

1.e4 a5 2.d4.strategy: Takes the centre at once. Black's 1...a5 does nothing for development or the middle of the board, so White occupies it with a second pawn and gains space, the initiative and a free choice of set-up.

1.e4 a5 2.Nf3.strategy: Develops without committing the centre pawns: the knight covers d4 and e5, so White can still build the full centre later or choose a slower set-up. Black's 1...a5 has not helped development, and White simply develops at a natural pace.

1.e4 a5 2.Nc3.strategy: Develops and guards e4, and the knight can head for b5, a square Black's a-pawn no longer controls, where it eyes c7 and d6. White keeps the d-pawn flexible and lets Black decide what the extra step on the wing is worth.

1.e4 a5 2.d4 Nc6.name: Ware Defence: Snagglepuss Defence
1.e4 a5 2.d4 Nc6.strategy: The first move since 1...a5 that does something useful: the knight develops and presses on d4, which the queen guards. Black still concedes the larger share of the centre and has to prove that the a-pawn move was worth the time.

1.e4 a5 2.d4 b6.strategy: Prepares to fianchetto the bishop and pressure e4, but White defends the pawn with a developing move and keeps the bigger centre and more space. Sound, but Black has made two flank moves and is the one catching up.

1.e4 a5 2.d4 e6.strategy: Answers the pawn centre solidly: a compact pawn chain, a free dark-squared bishop and ...d5 ready to challenge e4. 1...a5 has still developed nothing, so White keeps more space, but nothing in Black's position is weak.

1.e4 a5 2.d4 d5.strategy: Challenges e4 at once instead of waiting. White must either advance, which gains space but lets the light-squared bishop out, or exchange pawns. Sound, but it leaves Black a little behind in the fight for the centre.

1.e4 a6 2.d4.strategy: Takes the full centre and lets Black show what 1...a6 is for. Black has chosen to attack the centre from the flank instead of occupying it, so two central pawns are the natural answer and the test of that plan.

1.e4 a6 2.Nf3.strategy: Develops without committing the d-pawn: the knight covers d4 and e5, so White can still build the full centre or choose a slower set-up. Black's a6 has not yet shown its purpose, and the knight move lets White wait for it.

1.e4 a6 2.g3.strategy: Prepares to guard e4 from g2 with the fianchettoed bishop, which keeps the d-pawn and the knights free. A quiet, flexible set-up that avoids committing the centre, but it gives Black time to carry out the queenside plan unhindered.

1.e4 a6 2.d4 b5.strategy: Plays the idea of 1...a6 at once: the a-pawn guards b5 and the bishop will look at e4 from b7. But White's centre stays intact and the queenside is loosened, so White develops freely with a comfortable edge. Playable, but not the best use of the flank.

1.e4 a6 2.d4 e5.name: St. George Defence: Zilbermints Gambit
1.e4 a6 2.d4 e5.strategy: Gives up a pawn at once: after dxe5 Black has developed nothing and has no easy way to win it back, since Nf3 holds e5. Striking at the centre before any piece is out leaves White with the easier game.

1.e4 a6 2.d4 e6.strategy: Builds a compact pawn chain and prepares ...d5 to challenge e4, keeping the queenside advance in reserve. The a-pawn already keeps White's bishop off b5, so Black loses nothing by waiting. White has more space, but Black's position is solid and flexible.

1.e4 a6 2.d4 b5 3.Nf3.strategy: Develops and guards d4 while keeping the c-pawn free. The natural 3.Nc3 would run into ...b4, which drives the knight away and leaves e4 without support, so the knight goes to f3 and e4 is left for the bishop to hold.

1.e4 a6 2.d4 b5 3.Bd3.strategy: Defends e4 with a developing move and looks along the diagonal toward b5, which the a-pawn guards. The king's knight keeps its choice of square, so White builds the centre without hurrying the pieces.

1.e4 a6 2.d4 b5 3.c4.strategy: Attacks the b5 pawn with a third centre pawn, a gambit-like try to open the queenside before Black is ready. White builds a broad front but develops nothing and leaves e4 unguarded against a bishop on b7, so Black can answer calmly and fight for the open lines.

1.e4 a6 2.d4 b5 3.Nf3 Bb7.strategy: Develops with pressure on the undefended e4 pawn. Nc3 is not available as a defence because of ...b4, so White has to find another way to hold e4, while Black gains play along the long diagonal and on the queenside.

1.e4 a6 2.d4 b5 3.Nf3 e6.strategy: Builds a solid pawn chain and frees the dark-squared bishop, but gives up the immediate pressure on e4, so White gets time to put the pieces on good squares. The light-squared bishop can still come out on the long diagonal later.

1.e4 a6 2.d4 b5 3.Nf3 Nf6.strategy: Attacks e4 with a developing move, but the pawn simply advances with a gain of tempo and White takes space. Black gets active pieces for a space deficit and has to prove that the knight finds a good post after being chased.

1.e4 a6 2.d4 b5 3.Nf3 Bb7 4.Bd3.strategy: Defends e4 with a developing move and eyes the pawn on b5, the natural way to keep the broad centre. It is sound, but Black answers with easy development and ...e6, so White keeps only a small edge.

1.e4 a6 2.d4 b5 3.Nf3 Bb7 4.Nbd2.strategy: Guards e4 with the queen's knight, so the king's bishop develops freely and White's centre stays intact. The knight does block the c1-bishop, but the pawn centre and easy development matter more here.

1.e4 a6 2.d4 b5 3.Nf3 Bb7 4.Qe2.strategy: Defends e4 at once without moving a minor piece, but the queen blocks the king's bishop and White's development becomes awkward. The pawn holds, though White has to organise the pieces around a queen on e2.

1.e4 a6 2.d4 b5 3.Nf3 Bb7 4.Bd3 e6.name: St. George Defence: Polish Variation
1.e4 a6 2.d4 b5 3.Nf3 Bb7 4.Bd3 e6.strategy: The main line: a pawn on e6 takes d5 and f5 from White, opens the dark-squared bishop and prepares quick kingside development. Black builds a compact centre of their own rather than leaving White's pawns unopposed.

1.e4 a6 2.d4 b5 3.Nf3 Bb7 4.Bd3 d6.strategy: Holds e5 and prepares a classical set-up, but costs time: once White castles, the natural ...Nf6 runs into e5, which attacks the knight and leaves Black cramped. Black needs another way to develop, so White keeps the freer game.

1.e4 a6 2.d4 b5 3.Nf3 Bb7 4.Bd3 Nf6.strategy: Develops with pressure on e4, but the pressure is short-lived: White guards the pawn or drives the knight back with e5, and keeps the bigger centre. Sound, yet White chooses how the game goes.

1.e4 a6 2.d4 b5 3.Nf3 Bb7 4.Bd3 d6 5.O-O.strategy: Puts the king to safety at once. The bishop on d3 already protects e4, so White has no worries in the centre and can finish development before deciding how to meet Black's flank play.

1.e4 a6 2.d4 b5 3.Nf3 Bb7 4.Bd3 d6 5.Nbd.strategy: Brings the queen's knight into play and adds a second guard to e4, which frees the d3-bishop from that job. White keeps castling for later but accepts that the knight blocks the c1-bishop.

1.e4 a6 2.d4 b5 3.Nf3 Bb7 4.Bd3 d6 5.c3.strategy: Builds a solid centre: the pawn guards d4 and gives the d3-bishop the c2 retreat, so e4 and d4 stay protected without more piece moves. It takes c3 from the b1-knight, which must develop on d2, and the position stays quiet.

1.e4 a6 2.d4 b5 3.Nf3 Bb7 4.Bd3 d6 5.O-O.strategy: Prepares a second fianchetto, so that both bishops eye White's central pawns from the wings. Black concedes the centre completely and plans to undermine it from a distance, an offbeat and rather passive way to meet White's solid set-up.

The natural developing move, but it runs into e5: the pawn attacks the knight, and whether Black takes or retreats, White's space and active pieces give a clear advantage. The attack on e4 is over before it starts.

Builds a solid chain with d6 and frees the dark-squared bishop, leaving the knight free to choose its square. Black avoids the problem with ...Nf6, accepts that White has more space, and gets a compact position with few weaknesses.
Shores up d4 before the bishop on g7 can pressure it, and gives the d3-bishop the c2 retreat. It makes the centre solid but takes c3 from the b1-knight, which has to find another route.
Guards e4 and so frees the d3-bishop, while keeping the c-pawn flexible. White develops with pieces first against the double fianchetto and decides later whether to support d4 with a pawn.
Backs up e4 and the possible advance of that pawn with a rook behind it, now that the king is safe. It keeps the choice of route for the b1-knight open and builds the set-up in a harmonious order.

1.e4 a6 2.d4 b5 3.Nf3 Bb7 4.Bd3 d6 5.O-O.name: St. George Defence: San Jorge Variation
1.e4 a6 2.d4 b5 3.Nf3 Bb7 4.Bd3 d6 5.O-O.strategy: Completes the double fianchetto: the bishop on g7 joins the one on b7 in aiming at White's centre, presses on d4, and the king can castle behind a sound pawn shield. It is the move this set-up is built around, and the game stays solid, with Black's play coming from undermining White's pawns.

Adds a second attacker to e4 and develops toward castling, so White must support the pawn again or push it. Black shows that pressure on the centre can come from pieces as well as from the fianchettoed bishops.

Prepares the break ...e5 with a piece already guarding that square, but it gives up the pressure on e4 that a knight on f6 brings. A sound but slower way to develop that lets White organise the pieces unhindered.

1.e4 f6 2.d4.strategy: Takes the centre with a second pawn. Black's f6 neither develops a piece nor fights the centre: it takes the best square from the g8 knight and opens the e8–h5 diagonal against the king, and 2...e5 fails to 3.dxe5 fxe5 4.Qh5+ g6 5.Qxe5+.

1.e4 f6 2.Nf3.strategy: Develops and keeps d4 in reserve. It also sets a trap: 2...e5? loses a pawn, because after Nxe5 the recapture ...fxe5 runs into Qh5+ and Qxe5+, which forks king and rook.

1.e4 f6 2.Nc3.strategy: Develops and defends the e-pawn while keeping d4 available. It is sound, but it lets Black choose a set-up before White has claimed the centre; the weakness of the e8-h5 diagonal stays for White to use later.

1.e4 f6 2.d4 b6.strategy: Prepares ...Bb7, where the bishop eyes e4 along the long diagonal and fights the centre from a distance. It is a sensible development idea, but f6 has already weakened the kingside, and White has the whole centre to expand against.

1.e4 f6 2.d4 Kf7.name: Fried Fox Defence
1.e4 f6 2.d4 Kf7.strategy: Walks the king to f7, giving up castling: Bc4+ checks it at once, and the king stays exposed on that diagonal with White ahead in development. A real concession, but not a refutation.

1.e4 f6 2.d4 e6.strategy: The sensible way to develop: the pawn opens the bishop's diagonal and frees e7 for the g8 knight, since f6 is taken. Black can follow with ...d5 for a solid centre, and avoids 2...e5?, which loses a pawn. White keeps the space and the lead in development.

1.e4 f6 2.d4 Nc6.strategy: Develops the knight at once and attacks d4, but 3.d5 drives it away and gains space. The knight must retreat, and on e5 it can be chased again, so Black has lost time for no gain.

1.e4 f6 2.d4 g6.strategy: Gives the g8 knight the route h6 to f7, and the pawn on g6 shuts the e8-h5 diagonal for now. A Modern-style set-up that is playable, but White takes the centre with ease while Black's pieces are still behind their pawns.

1.e4 f6 2.d4 b6 3.c4.strategy: Builds a broad centre: the c-pawn joins d4 and e4 and controls d5, so the bishop has no easy outpost. White keeps an edge, but a smaller one than with a developing move, and e4 needs a piece to guard it once the bishop arrives on b7.

1.e4 f6 2.d4 b6 3.Bd3.strategy: Defends the e-pawn in advance and develops in the same move, so the bishop on b7 will have nothing to bite on. White keeps the full centre and only has to bring the pieces up, while Black's f6 pawn keeps the g8 knight from its best square.

1.e4 f6 2.d4 b6 3.Nc3.strategy: Develops and guards e4 as well. The knight blocks the c-pawn, so White gives up the broad c4 centre, in exchange for quick development and a firm hold on the centre squares.

1.e4 f6 2.d4 b6 3.c4 Bb7.name: Owen's Defence: Unicorn Variation
1.e4 f6 2.d4 b6 3.c4 Bb7.strategy: Develops the bishop on the long diagonal and attacks the undefended e4 pawn, the point of ...b6. White defends with a developing move and keeps the broad centre, so the attack gains little; striking at the centre with a pawn at once is more testing.

1.e4 f6 2.d4 b6 3.c4 e6.strategy: Takes space and frees e7 for the g8 knight, the development problem that ...f6 created. The light-squared bishop keeps the long diagonal for ...Bb7, so the plan of ...b6 keeps its point, but White's centre stays the larger one.

1.e4 f6 2.d4 b6 3.c4 g6.strategy: Shuts the e8-h5 diagonal and prepares Bg7, which makes the king safer. It is another pawn move before a piece is out, though, and White's big centre gains time to expand.

1.e4 f6 2.d4 b6 3.c4 e5.strategy: Strikes at the broad centre at once: the pawn attacks d4, so White has to deal with it. Black gets open lines for its pieces instead of waiting, and it is the most active way to meet the wide centre, though White keeps the better game.

1.e4 g5 2.d4.strategy: Attacks the loose pawn at once: the bishop on c1 now sees g5 and nothing defends it. White takes the centre with tempo while Black's kingside pawn move has weakened the position and cost time.

1.e4 g5 2.Nf3.strategy: Develops and attacks the loose g5 pawn at once, so Black has to defend it. ...g4 only drives the knight to e5, from where it attacks the pawn again. White gains a tempo for development and keeps the initiative.

1.e4 g5 2.Nc3.strategy: Develops and supports e4, but leaves the g5 pawn alone, so Black gets time to develop and settle. Sound, though it passes up the chance to make Black react.

1.e4 g5 2.d4 h6.strategy: Defends the attacked pawn with another pawn and holds on to the material. Black keeps the plan of a fianchettoed bishop but has spent two wing pawn moves with no piece out, so White's lead in development and space is the price.

1.e4 g5 2.d4 Bg7.name: Borg Defence: Borg Gambit
1.e4 g5 2.d4 Bg7.strategy: Ignores the attack on g5 and hits the d4 pawn with the fianchettoed bishop. The queen defends d4, so White can simply take the g-pawn, and Black must find enough activity and development to justify the pawn.

1.e4 g5 2.d4 e5.name: Borg Defence: Zilbermints Gambit
1.e4 g5 2.d4 e5.strategy: Offers a central pawn: the queen now guards g5, but White simply takes on e5 and is a pawn up with the better centre. A gambit without clear compensation.

1.e4 g5 2.d4 h6 3.h4.strategy: Attacks g5 a second time, so Black has to act at once. If Black takes on h4, the rook recaptures and presses on the h-file while Black's broken kingside stays weak. The cost is a rook's pawn advanced before any piece is out, which loosens White's own kingside.

1.e4 g5 2.d4 h6 3.Nf3.strategy: Develops, guards d4 and adds a second attacker to g5, which the h6 pawn holds alone. Sound and natural, but slower than the moves that go for the weakened kingside or the centre at once; Black gets time to consolidate.

1.e4 g5 2.d4 h6 3.c3.strategy: Props up d4 before the bishop arrives on g7, so the centre is safe, and ...g4 would lose a pawn to the queen. Safe but passive: no piece is developed, the knight loses the c3 square, and Black gets time to organise.

1.e4 g5 2.d4 h6 3.Bd3.strategy: Defends e4 with a developing move and keeps both knights free, but the bishop blocks the queen's guard of d4, so that pawn stands unprotected. Sound, yet Black gets time to hit the centre, and White gives up the quicker ways to use the weakened kingside.

1.e4 g5 2.d4 h6 3.Nc3.strategy: Develops the knight, protects e4 and keeps every plan open, the h-pawn lunge included. White builds quietly while Black's kingside pawns, already pushed and loosened by ...g5 and ...h6, stay a long-term target and Black has no active counter.

1.e4 g5 2.d4 h6 3.h4 g4.name: Borg Defence: Troon Gambit
1.e4 g5 2.d4 h6 3.h4 g4.strategy: Pushes the attacked pawn past White's h-pawn instead of taking it, which cramps White's kingside. The pawn is exposed on g4 with nothing to guard it, so White can win it with the queen or just develop with a clear edge. Playable, but a step behind taking on h4.

1.e4 g5 2.d4 h6 3.h4 gxh4.strategy: The only move that keeps the material level: Black takes the pawn that attacks g5. After Rxh4 the rook and the c1-bishop both press on h6, but three black pieces guard it. White keeps the lead in development.

1.e4 g5 2.d4 h6 3.h4 Bg7.strategy: Develops and guards the h8 rook, but gives up a pawn: after hxg5 hxg5 Rxh8 Bxh8, White simply takes on g5. The kingside weakened by ...g5 costs Black material.

1.e4 g5 2.d4 h6 3.h4 Nf6.strategy: Develops a piece but ignores the h-file: after hxg5, hxg5 leaves the rook on h8 attacked by White's rook with nothing to recapture, so Rxh8 wins it. Black must decline the recapture and is a pawn down with a loosened position.

1.e4 h5 2.d4.strategy: Takes the centre and leaves Black's rook-pawn move as a wasted tempo that also weakens the kingside. White is ahead in space and development and just needs to play normally.

1.e4 h5 2.Nc3.strategy: Develops a piece toward the centre and supports e4 and a later d4, while Black's rook-pawn move has done nothing for development or the centre. White just plays natural moves and keeps the lead in time.

1.e4 h5 2.Nf3.strategy: Develops the knight, covers d4 and e5 and prepares kingside castling, using the tempo Black spent on the edge pawn. Black gains space on the wing but nothing in the centre.

1.e4 h5 2.d4 Nf6.name: Goldsmith Defence: Picklepuss Defence
1.e4 h5 2.d4 Nf6.strategy: The natural developing reply, which hits e4. Black has not made up the tempo spent on h5, so White keeps the centre and a pleasant edge, but the position is sound.

1.e4 h5 2.d4 d5.strategy: Challenges the centre at once. White can push past the pawn for space, and the rook-pawn move has done nothing for the fight in the middle, but the bishop on c8 is free to come out and the position stays solid.

1.e4 h5 2.d4 d6.strategy: A compact set-up: the pawn holds e5 and frees the c8 bishop. White gets the centre and the first move, but Black has a solid game and can undermine it later, and the tempo spent on h5 hurts little.

1.e4 h6 2.d4.strategy: Takes the centre against a move that develops nothing and fights for nothing. White builds a pawn centre and develops with an edge.

1.e4 h6 2.Nf3.strategy: Develops with a purpose: the knight eyes e5 and d4 and clears the way for castling. White simply makes natural moves and lets Black's wasted rook-pawn move count against Black, keeping the choice between a broad centre and slower play.

1.e4 h6 2.Nc3.strategy: Develops and defends e4, which keeps the centre pawn safe while White decides how to build. It blocks the c-pawn and commits the knight early, so it is a little less flexible than a knight on f3, but Black's h6 gives no real counterplay.

1.e4 h6 2.d4 e5.name: Carr Defence: Zilbermints Gambit
1.e4 h6 2.d4 e5.strategy: Offers the e-pawn to open the centre at once, but Black has not a single piece out. After the pawn is taken, White has an extra pawn and the lead in development, and open lines favour the side ahead in development.

1.e4 h6 2.d4 d5.strategy: Challenges the centre at once, but 3.exd5 Qxd5 4.Nc3 gains a tempo against the queen and gives White the lead in development. Black stays solid, and the rook-pawn move at least takes g5 from the dark-squared bishop.

1.e4 h6 2.d4 Nf6.strategy: Attacks e4 and develops, but 3.e5 drives the knight back at once and gains space with tempo. The knight loses time wherever it goes, and the pawn on h6 does nothing for development.

1.e4 h6 2.d4 d6.strategy: A compact defence: the pawn holds e5 and opens the bishop on c8. White gets the space and the initiative, but Black has a solid game, and the tempo spent on h6 can be made up later.

1.e4 h6 2.d4 e6.strategy: Prepares ...d5 with a solid pawn on e6 and so contests the centre safely. The bishop on c8 stays hemmed in for now, but the compact structure absorbs the tempo spent on h6, and White's edge is small.

1.e4 Nh6 2.d4.strategy: Takes the whole centre, since the knight on the rim has no useful way to attack it. White gets a freer game, and Black has to justify the odd development with counterplay later.

1.e4 Nh6 2.Nf3.strategy: Develops a piece without committing in the centre and keeps the d-pawn free to move when it suits. White completes development comfortably while Black's knight stays on the rim, with no good square: a knight to f5 is simply taken by the e-pawn.

1.e4 Nh6 2.Nc3.strategy: Develops a piece and adds control of the centre. It is sound but blocks the c-pawn and takes no space yet, so White uses less of the advantage that the misplaced knight on h6 offers.

1.e4 Nh6 2.d4 g6.strategy: Answers the problem of the knight on h6: the c1-bishop eyes it after 2.d4, but with the pawn on g6 the king's bishop guards it, so Bxh6 Bxh6 only trades pieces and leaves Black's pawns intact. It prepares a fianchetto and play against the centre from a distance, though White keeps the space edge.

1.e4 Nh6 2.d4 d5.strategy: Takes a share of the centre at once, but leaves the knight on h6 to be traded: Bxh6 gxh6 gives Black doubled pawns on the h-file and a loosened kingside, even if Black keeps the two bishops. A long-term structural problem for an otherwise natural move.

1.e4 Nh6 2.d4 d6.strategy: A modest, solid move that frees the c8 bishop and keeps the centre flexible. It leaves Black with the same structural problem, since Bxh6 gxh6 damages the kingside pawns, and White holds the larger centre.

1.e4 Nh6 2.d4 c6.strategy: Prepares ...d5, a solid stand against White's centre. If White trades on h6, Black gets the bishop pair for doubled pawns on the h-file; White keeps a space edge.
